title: Great Zimbabwe’s 11-metre walls were built without a drop of mortar
body: Between the 11th and 15th centuries, ancestors of the Shona people built a stone city in what is now Zimbabwe. Its Great Enclosure has dry-stone walls up to **11 metres high** running for about 250 metres, laid without mortar, and the site is the largest stone structure in precolonial southern Africa. Rhodesia’s colonial government later pressured archaeologists to deny that Africans had built it and censored those who disagreed, though scholars had settled the question by the 1950s. The modern nation took its name from the ruins: Dzimba-dze-mabwe, ‘large houses of stone’.

slides.question: How high do the Great Enclosure’s dry-stone walls rise?
slides.explanation: Up to 11 metres, built in the 13th and 14th centuries from stones fitted together with no mortar at all.

slides.label: the height of the Great Enclosure’s dry-stone walls, raised in the 13th and 14th centuries
slides.text: They extend for roughly 250 metres with no mortar at all: the stones are simply fitted together.

slides.heading: Walls and tower of the Great Enclosure, in metres
slides.note: The outer wall runs for about 250 m; the Conical Tower stands between the inner and outer walls.

events.text: Major construction, from the Hill Complex to the Great Enclosure
UNESCO lists Great Zimbabwe as a World Heritage Site

left.label: Colonial claim
left.text: Rhodesia’s official line in the 1960s and 70s: the walls were the work of outsiders, not Black Africans. Archaeologists who disagreed were censored.

right.label: The evidence
right.text: The first scientific excavations, in 1905–06, pointed to the ancestors of the Shona; by the 1950s that was the scholarly consensus.

slides.heading: The Zimbabwe Birds
slides.text: The most important finds from the site are eight birds carved from soapstone. When the country took the site’s name in 1980, the bird became a national symbol, and it appears on Zimbabwe’s flag today.
